name: Grüner Veltliner

lines.s10: Grüner Veltliner is the white Austria is known for: crisp green apple and lime with a twist of white pepper, dry and mouthwatering.
lines.s20: Grüner Veltliner is the white grape of Austria, grown along the Danube and north of Vienna. It is dry and brisk, with green apple, lime and a peppery, savoury edge that makes it easy to pour with almost any dish.
lines.s45: Grüner Veltliner is the peppery one. It is Austria's native white grape, grown along the Danube west of Vienna and across the rolling country to the north. It tastes of green apple, lime and white peach, with a snap of white pepper and a green note like celery. It is dry, with bright acidity, and it runs from light and brisk to rich and full. Most of it is made in steel or big old casks, with no new oak. Try it with a schnitzel, asparagus or anything fried. Austrians have a word for that peppery snap: Pfefferl, the little pepper.
lines.sale: Grüner Veltliner gets on with the green things that trouble other wines, asparagus and artichoke among them. With the first courses, its lime and white pepper meet every green plate on the table.

glass.lead: Green apple, lime and white peach with a snap of white pepper and a green note of lentil and celery, dry and brisk.

ladder.where: The Weinviertel, the Kamptal and the cooler, higher Wachau
Sun warmed Danube terraces, picked late as Smaragd

glass.structure: Dry. Acidity high, alcohol moderate, body light to medium; fuller and stronger in a Smaragd or a reserve.

home.home: Austria, above all Niederösterreich: the broad Weinviertel north of Vienna, and the Wachau, Kamptal and Kremstal along the Danube. Most is fermented in steel or large old casks and sold young, light and peppery. Riper grapes from the steep Danube terraces give fuller, longer lived wines, the Wachau's Smaragd among them.
home.abroad: Its neighbours grow it too: Slovakia, the Czech Republic and Hungary. A little is grown in Alto Adige's Isarco Valley, New Zealand, the Adelaide Hills and the Finger Lakes, and bottled under the grape's own name.

service.temp: 45 to 50 degrees Fahrenheit, 7 to 10 degrees Celsius; a rich Smaragd a few degrees warmer.
service.glass: A white wine glass; a wider bowl suits a rich, mature Smaragd.
service.decant: Usually unnecessary; a young, powerful Smaragd can open with a short decant, so taste a sample first.
service.age: Most within two or three years; a Smaragd or a reserve rewards five and can keep far longer.

labels.means: The Wachau's three weights of dry white, from light to rich; Smaragd is the ripest and fullest.
Austria's first protected regional style, from the 2002 vintage: dry, peppery Grüner Veltliner alone.
Districts beside the Wachau whose protected dry whites are Grüner Veltliner or Riesling.
On an Austrian label, a riper, fuller dry wine released later.

guest.q: I usually drink Sauvignon Blanc. Will I like this?
guest.a: Very likely. It is just as dry and fresh, with lime and green apple, but where Sauvignon Blanc is grassy this is peppery, and a little rounder.
A little: a prickle of white pepper on the finish, not heat. Austrians call it the Pfefferl, and it shows most in the light, young wines of the Weinviertel.

guest.q: What does Smaragd mean on the label?
guest.a: It is the Wachau's word for its ripest, fullest dry wines, named for the emerald green lizard that suns itself on the terrace walls. Federspiel is the lighter style.

compare.tell: Dry Riesling is lime, white peach and, with age, petrol, on sharper acidity; Grüner Veltliner is peppery and green, with lentil and celery.
Sauvignon Blanc is grassy, with gooseberry and passion fruit; Grüner Veltliner is quieter, with white pepper, lentil and a rounder middle.
Albariño is salty, with peach and apricot; Grüner Veltliner has green apple, lime and a white pepper finish, with no note of sea salt.

cards.front: Grüner Veltliner: where is home, and what gives it away blind?
cards.back: Austria, above all Niederösterreich. White pepper with lentil, green bean and celery over green apple and lime, dry, with high acidity and no new oak.

cards.front: Grüner Veltliner in the Wachau: name its three styles, from light to rich.
cards.back: Steinfeder, Federspiel and Smaragd. Smaragd is the ripest and fullest, named for the emerald lizard of the terrace walls, and the one that rewards keeping.

cards.front: Grüner Veltliner: who are its parents, and how was one found?
cards.back: Traminer and a vine known as St. Georgen. A single old plant was found in 2000 at St. Georgen in Burgenland, and DNA work showed it to be the missing parent.

questions.q: A blind white is pale with green tints, dry and unoaked, with green apple, lime, a prickle of white pepper and a note of lentil. The acidity is high. Which grape is it most likely to be?
questions.exp: White pepper with lentil and green bean over lime and green apple is the mark of Grüner Veltliner. Sauvignon Blanc would be grassy, with gooseberry or passion fruit, and Albariño salty and peachy.

questions.q: A guest asks for the ripest, fullest dry white the Wachau makes. Which word on the label do you look for?
questions.exp: Smaragd is the Wachau's ripest, fullest dry style. Federspiel is the middle weight and Steinfeder the light one, and Kabinett is not one of the Wachau's three.

questions.q: A table has ordered artichokes with lemon and then asparagus, and asks for one dry white for both. Which do you pour?
questions.exp: A dry, fresh Grüner Veltliner with no new oak, and with green, peppery notes of its own, is the model choice with artichoke and asparagus. Heavy new oak, or a rich, low acid white such as Condrieu or white Hermitage, would crowd both dishes.

report: Mode home, as the plan fixes it: Austria is the list, and abroad names its neighbours and a few small New World bottlings without claiming a second style.
No respelling stands in the Court's grid for this grape; the say line gives the German F for the V of Veltliner.

The parentage, a natural cross of Traminer and the St. Georgen vine, stands on the Austrian wine body; the year 2000 for the finding of the single old vine is the most common date in the references read, and one glossary dates the DNA proof to 2007, so the card gives the finding and no year for the proof.
The lentil, green bean, celery and radish notes are the reviewed profile's own; white pepper as Pfefferl is the Austrian wine body's and the Codex's Weinviertel record's.

Abroad: Slovakia, the Czech Republic and Hungary stand on two general references; the Finger Lakes, Marlborough and Sopron are named for the grape in the Codex's own region records; Alto Adige's Isarco Valley and the Adelaide Hills each on one trade reference, so a checker may wish to confirm them.
Left out: the London tasting of 2002 in which Grüner Veltliner was set against Chardonnay, since its organisers are living; any figure for Austria's share of the grape.
The sources were read through search results; this session could not open the hosts directly.

checked.verdict: Sound after three fixes. The parentage (Traminer and the St. Georgen vine, found in 2000), the Weinviertel rule from the 2002 vintage and every place under abroad were confirmed.
changed: questions[2].opts: the stem asks for one dry white and two options were sweet wines, so only two were live. All four are now dry whites: the key, an oaked Napa Valley Chardonnay, Condrieu and white Hermitage. The explanation follows.
cards[1].front and questions[1].exp: the word the lint read as a superlative is reworded (from light to rich; the light one), which clears both notes.
open: Ginger stands in the spice group beside white pepper: a note of ripe Smaragd, not of the light wines.
The Adelaide Hills and Alto Adige's Isarco Valley, which the author asked a checker to confirm, are confirmed. The Finger Lakes stands on the Codex's own region record.
